blocks.text: ZeRO-2 extends ZeRO-1, covered in the previous topic, by additionally sharding gradients across devices, not just optimizer state, addressing a second VRAM consumer covered in the earlier VRAM Management topic while model weights themselves remain fully replicated, one step short of ZeRO-3 covered next.
This topic explains exactly what ZeRO-2 adds on top of ZeRO-1, and the modest additional overhead that comes with sharding one more consumer.
1. What ZeRO Stage 2 Adds

blocks.alt: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, and ZeRO-2 adds sharding gradients too

blocks.text: ZeRO-2 takes everything ZeRO-1 already does, sharding optimizer state, and adds gradient sharding on top, meaning each device now holds only a portion of both the optimizer state and the gradients, rather than a full replicated copy of either.
2. Sharding Gradients in Addition to Optimizer State

blocks.alt: Optimizer state and gradients both get sharded under ZeRO-2 while model weights remain replicated

blocks.text: Gradients, covered in the Optimizer States topic as one of the four VRAM consumers, require memory roughly proportional to the trainable parameter count, and sharding them across devices, the same way ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, delivers an additional memory reduction on top of what ZeRO-1 alone achieves.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch of ZeRO-2 gradient sharding, extending ZeRO-1
device_optimizer_shard = optimizer_state[device_rank::num_devices]
device_gradient_shard = gradients[device_rank::num_devices]
# Both are now sharded, only model weights remain fully replicated

blocks.text: 3. ZeRO-2 Memory Savings Over ZeRO-1

blocks.alt: ZeRO-1 saves on optimizer state only while ZeRO-2 saves on optimizer state plus gradients

blocks.text: Since gradients add their own meaningful memory cost on top of optimizer state, ZeRO-2 delivers a larger total memory reduction than ZeRO-1 alone, particularly valuable for training setups where both consumers together represent a significant share of total memory usage.

blocks.text: 4. ZeRO-2 Communication Pattern

blocks.alt: The backward pass leads through gradient shard communication to the applied update

blocks.text: Because gradients are now sharded rather than fully replicated, ZeRO-2 requires additional coordination during the backward pass to correctly combine gradient shards from across devices before applying the weight update, communication ZeRO-1 alone does not need.
5. ZeRO-2's Additional Overhead

blocks.alt: The extra gradient sync in ZeRO-2 adds only modest additional overhead

blocks.text: The additional communication ZeRO-2 introduces beyond ZeRO-1 is generally modest relative to the extra memory savings it provides, making it a reasonable next step up when ZeRO-1 memory savings alone are not quite sufficient for a given training setup.

blocks.title: This progression mirrors the VRAM Management framework directly
blocks.content: ZeRO-1 targets optimizer state, ZeRO-2 adds gradients, and ZeRO-3, covered next, adds model weights, precisely mapping onto the four VRAM consumers introduced in the earlier VRAM Management topic, minus activations, which gradient checkpointing addresses separately.

blocks.text: 6. ZeRO-2 vs ZeRO-1, When to Move Up

blocks.alt: If only optimizer state is the bottleneck, ZeRO-1 is enough, otherwise consider ZeRO-2

blocks.text: The decision to move from ZeRO-1 to ZeRO-2 comes down to whether optimizer state sharding alone was sufficient, if a training setup still runs into memory limits after enabling ZeRO-1, checking whether gradient memory is contributing to that remaining pressure points toward moving up to ZeRO-2.
7. ZeRO-2 and Training Stability

ZeRO-2, like ZeRO-1, is mathematically equivalent to standard data parallel training, it simply distributes where data lives rather than changing the underlying training computation, meaning it should not introduce any training stability concerns beyond the normal considerations covered throughout this course.
8. ZeRO-2 in Practice

Like ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2 is typically enabled through a simple configuration change within DeepSpeed or another supporting framework, selecting stage two rather than stage one, without needing any change to the underlying training code itself.
9. ZeRO-2 as a Middle Ground

blocks.alt: ZeRO-2 sits as a middle ground between ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-3

blocks.text: ZeRO-2 occupies a natural middle ground in this progression, more memory savings than ZeRO-1 with only modest additional overhead, but not yet the maximum memory savings, and correspondingly higher communication cost, that ZeRO-3 covered in the next topic provides.
Worked Example

A team already using ZeRO-1 finds their training still runs close to their memory limit, particularly noticeable when working with a larger model where gradient memory has grown meaningfully alongside optimizer state.

Moving up to ZeRO-2, sharding gradients in addition to the optimizer state ZeRO-1 already shards, frees up enough additional memory to comfortably fit their training run, with only a modest increase in communication overhead compared to their previous ZeRO-1 setup.
Common Mistakes

items: Jumping straight to ZeRO-3 without first checking whether ZeRO-2 alone would have provided sufficient memory savings
Not recognizing gradient memory as a contributing factor when ZeRO-1 alone proves insufficient
Assuming ZeRO-2 shards model weights, when weights remain fully replicated until ZeRO-3
Overlooking the modest but real additional communication overhead ZeRO-2 introduces beyond ZeRO-1

blocks.text: Practice

For a training setup already using ZeRO-1 that still runs into memory limits, sketch how much additional memory sharding gradients under ZeRO-2 might free up, given the trainable parameter count of your chosen model.
Key Takeaway

ZeRO-2 extends ZeRO-1 by additionally sharding gradients across devices, delivering greater memory savings than optimizer state sharding alone at the cost of modest additional communication overhead, and it serves as a natural middle ground between the more conservative ZeRO-1 and the maximum memory savings ZeRO-3 provides by also sharding model weights themselves.
